title: Willing Hands
logline: A village turns out to clear a tank bund or temple ground together. Some people arrived because they wanted to. Others came because they were asked, and their whole day moves differently.

object.note: Object 3 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: The tank carries across: after the argument over its water, a village turns out to clear a bund, some because they wanted to, some because they were asked.

thread_out.thread: From a day where pushed and willing hands move differently to a person who knows in the body what the old heat felt like, and no longer goes there.

requirements: A village organising a genuine communal work day during the filming window
A mix of participants who came for different reasons, willing to speak plainly about it

lesson.in_simple_terms: The same job can feel light or heavy depending on whether we chose it or were pushed into it. Describing unhelpful states of mind, the old texts notice something similar: heaviness and dullness show up only when a mind had to be urged along.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: කැමැත්තෙන් කරන වැඩට වඩා බලකිරීමකින් කරන වැඩ බර දැනෙනවා සේම, අලස බව හා මැලිකම ඇතිවන්නේ මෙහෙයවීමෙන් උපදින අකුසල් සිත්වල පමණක් බව ධර්මය කියයි.
lesson.the_teaching: The texts teach that sloth and torpor (thīna-middha), the mind's shrinking and heaviness, occur only in unwholesome minds that arise with urging (sasaṅkhārika), never in spontaneous ones, because they make the mind unfit for the task at hand. Pradeepika's image is a bird's feather curling away from a flame. It also separates this mental dullness from the body's honest need for rest after travel or illness, which even the fully awakened share.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The film follows the day from the morning gathering into the afternoon heat: who sets the pace, who lingers over tea, who drifts to the shade and who returns quickly to the work. The difference between eager and asked-for effort shows in bodies and pacing rather than words, and people say in their own words why they came.

key_terms.en: sloth of mind / torpor of mental factors

lesson.caution: This does not mean that people who came because they were asked are doing wrong, or that tiredness in the heat is laziness; the source describes harmful states of mind, and the link here is only an analogy.
lesson.builds_on: The water meeting showed two ways a mind grips in argument; after it, the same village turns out to work, and the lesson shifts from what the mind grips to how heavy it becomes when it is pushed.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
